transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, D.C., I'm Dale Willman.
In Brazil, left-wing President Lula has come from behind to win the presidential election
there after ranking second in an initial round of voting.
Catherine Osborn reports from Rio de Janeiro.
A downtown Rio Plaza pulsed with surprise relief after President Luis Inácio Lula da
Silva was elected for a fourth nonconsecutive term.
He defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Shair Bolsonaro.
The possibility of another Bolsonaro presidency sent Lula supporters into the streets to campaign
by the tens of thousands in recent weeks.
Their attempt to swing votes paid off.
Lula's victory runs counter to a right-wing wave sweeping Latin America.
He's promised to continue standing up to President Trump's aggressive approach toward the region.
For NPR News, I'm Catherine Osborn in Rio de Janeiro.
President Trump campaigned in Michigan Sunday where he intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric
against U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
At a rally in Port Huron, he falsely called El-Sayed a jihadist who's on the side of
terrorists and he said he would need to go through a metal detector before he could ever
enter the center chamber.
Those comments were quickly denounced by Bishara Baba, who founded Arab Americans for Trump.
He called them racist.
Attorney General Todd Blanche says President Trump was right to order a lawsuit to block
the certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan
loses.
That's because there's a second Dan Sullivan also in the race.
Speaking on CNN Sunday, Blanche says that's confusing.
In our system, we should not have a candidate who has to worry about another candidate being
on the ballot for no other reason than to confuse voters.
And so it's something the Department of Justice has been looking at for a while.
The non-incumbent Dan Sullivan says he's not running to help Democrats.
The Alaska Supreme Court has already turned down a Republican challenge.
The Israeli army has sealed off the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank and is forcibly
evicting Palestinians from some of its neighborhoods.
This comes in response to an attack by two Palestinians on an Israeli checkpoint last
week.
Two soldiers were killed in that attack.
NPR's Ruth Sherlock has more on our story.
Analysts say Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's decision to retaliate with such force is an
attempt to show strength, as he struggles to gain a majority in the polls ahead of Tuesday's
elections in Israel.
Local authorities in Hebron in the occupied West Bank say the Israeli military has forcibly
removed more than 2,000 Palestinians from their homes.
The evictions have focused on the neighborhoods that the Palestinians who attacked the military
checkpoint came from.
The army has also placed the entire city on lockdown.
The group Physicians for Human Rights Israel says the restrictions of movement are forcing
Palestinian medical crews to transfer patients between vehicles at checkpoints and is delaying
access to hospitals.
Ruth Sherlock, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
And you're listening to NPR News.
Hollywood had another strong weekend in theaters, and NPR's Bob Mondello says the top films
all have something in common.
When it comes to this week's box office leaders, there will be blood, as it were. In Clayface,
a DC Comics adaptation that took the top spot, the lead character's blood is filled with
nanotech agents that cause him to change shape.
What's happening to me?
In You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder's runner-up at the box office, it's convicted
fraudster Elizabeth Holmes and her blood testing scam that are central.
You really feel you did nothing wrong?
I did not.
An infusion of 1,800 new screens helped You Can See Everything come close in its second
weekend to topping the opening of the well-reviewed supervillain movie.
The almost three-hour documentary remains in fewer theaters than Clayface, but it played
to more patrons per theater.
Bob Mondello, NPR News.
The iconic musical Rent is celebrating its 30th anniversary on Monday with a special
benefit performance.
Several original cast members will be returning to the stage and the event will be livestreamed.
The proceeds will be given to the group Broadway Cares, Equity Fights Aids.
The musical explores themes of poverty, drug use, and AIDS in New York's East Village.
After eight weeks of college football, the AP Top 10 has seen some changes.
Miami stays in first for another week, while Ohio State moves up one slot, following BYU's
loss to UCF.
One lost Georgia moves back up to number three, and Indiana lands in fourth.
Notre Dame drops one after a loss week to BYU, while Utah jumps four slots to sixth after
a win over Houston, UCLA is in seventh, followed by BYU, Kentucky, and Alabama.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.

topics.text: Lula wins Brazil's presidential election over Flavio Bolsonaro after trailing in the first round
Trump intensifies anti-Muslim rhetoric at Michigan rally against Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed
Attorney General Todd Blanche backs Trump lawsuit over Alaska Senate results and duplicate Dan Sullivan candidate
Israeli army seals off Hebron in occupied West Bank and evicts over 2,000 Palestinians after checkpoint attack
Clayface and Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes documentary lead weekend box office
Rent marks 30th anniversary with livestreamed benefit performance benefiting Broadway Cares
AP college football Top 10 shake-up as Miami holds first and Ohio State rises after BYU loss
